No, that isn't right, and it matters for your design. A language model doesn't remember earlier conversations on its own. Each call starts blank, and the model only knows what is in the text you send it that time.

Chatbot apps seem to remember because the app does the remembering. It keeps the earlier messages and sends them back with every new message.

Here is how that plays out in your makerspace assistant:

- Last week, a student tells it, "I finished the laser cutter safety training."
- This week, that student starts a new session. The model has nothing from last week unless your code puts it there.
- To make it work, your code saves the fact somewhere, such as a JSON file or a small database keyed by student. At the start of the next session, it reads the record and includes it in the prompt, for example "Student 4821: laser cutter training completed Nov 3."

So memory is a feature you design. You decide what to save, where to keep it, and what to put back in the prompt. Every token you put back also costs money, which matters with your small budget.

It's a common mix-up because chat apps hide this work well. Within one conversation, the "memory" is just the transcript being resent each turn.

Quick check: in your own words, if a student returns next week and your code sends the model only their new question, what will the model know about them?

If you'd like, I can turn this into a lesson on context and memory. That is the next topic in your mission, and it covers what to keep in context, what to save between sessions, and how to find the right page in a long manual.
